entries.title: Why the Maps of London, Tokyo, New York, and Other Major Cities Look the Way They Do
entries.summary: If you’re trying to understand a city, its map isn’t a bad place to start. Today, of course, we can call up an accurate map of practically any part of any city at any time we like, with detailed point-to-point directions available on command. Turn on the satellite view, street view, or 3D mode with […]
entries.content:
If you’re try­ing to under­stand a city, its map isn’t a bad place to start. Today, of course, we can call up an accu­rate map of prac­ti­cal­ly any part of any city at any time we like, with detailed point-to-point direc­tions avail­able on com­mand. Turn on the satel­lite view, street view, or 3D mode with its offer of every imag­in­able point of view, and you soon feel you’re engag­ing with less a rep­re­sen­ta­tion of the city than the city itself. Yet the famil­iar­i­ty this makes us feel we pos­sess is decep­tive, a real­iza­tion that comes afresh when­ev­er our phone runs out of bat­tery, leav­ing us bare­ly able to find our way through even neigh­bor­hoods we’d thought we knew. Sheer habit can get us between the places we fre­quent, but that’s a far cry indeed from under­stand­ing the city as a whole.

That last is just what YouTu­ber Daniel Stein­er attempts to do in his series of map explain­ers, which draws con­nec­tions between the large-scale, abstract­ed view of the map and the con­crete expe­ri­ence down on the street. He not only uses maps both cur­rent and his­tor­i­cal to illu­mi­nate why the street net­work and neigh­bor­hood bound­aries of a giv­en city have tak­en the shape they have, but actu­al­ly trav­els to that city and meets with experts equipped to point out phys­i­cal traces of that process of urban evo­lu­tion that escape the atten­tion of most locals.

Those could be the infra­struc­tur­al rem­nants of Roman Lon­don (or rather Lon­dini­um); the unloved Tokyo over­pass where the major roads of old Japan once con­verged; the sur­vey­or’s rod from the orig­i­nal grid­ding of Man­hat­tan stick­ing out of what’s now Cen­tral Park; or the con­tours of Ams­ter­dam even before its famous canals went in.

One vis­it to a city, of course, can hard­ly an under­stand­ing make. Stein­er has so far returned to New York to cre­ate addi­tion­al videos focus­ing on Broad­way, Brook­lyn, the Bronx, and Stat­en Island, and his exam­i­na­tion of Los Ange­les ends with a call for requests for more sub­jects to cov­er with­in the vast odd­i­ty of the south­ern Cal­i­for­nia metrop­o­lis. His map explain­ers on oth­er Amer­i­can cities from Chica­go to Seat­tle to Savan­nah, Geor­gia also show great poten­tial for fol­low-ups, to say noth­ing of how deep he could get into Mex­i­co City after hav­ing told the sto­ry of how it used to be a lake. Part of these cities’ appeal lies in the fact that, no mat­ter how long you spend in them, you can nev­er get to know them com­plete­ly, irre­sistible though it is to try. To the ques­tion of whether that attempt is best made top-down or bot­tom-up, Stein­er’s videos respond implic­it­ly — and con­vinc­ing­ly — why not both?

Relat­ed con­tent:

A Won­der­ful Archive of His­toric Tran­sit Maps: Expres­sive Art Meets Pre­cise Graph­ic Design

The Genius Urban Design of Ams­ter­dam: Canals, Dams & Lean­ing Hous­es

136 Maps Reveal Where Tourists & Locals Take Pho­tos in Major Cities Across the Globe

Japan­ese Design­er Cre­ates Incred­i­bly Detailed & Real­is­tic Maps of a City That Doesn’t Exist

Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

entries.title: It’s the End of the World as We Know It: The Apocalypse Gets Visualized in an Inventive Map from 1486
entries.summary: When will the world end? We can find serious scientific answers to this question, depending on what we mean by “world” and “end.” If we mean the end of civilization as we currently know it, climate scientists’ worst-case scenario points toward somewhere around 2100 as the beginning of the end. (New York magazine points out that […]
entries.content:
When will the world end?

We can find seri­ous sci­en­tif­ic answers to this ques­tion, depend­ing on what we mean by “world” and “end.” If we mean the end of civ­i­liza­tion as we cur­rent­ly know it, cli­mate sci­en­tists’ worst-case sce­nario points toward some­where around 2100 as the begin­ning of the end. (New York mag­a­zine points out that it “prob­a­bly won’t kill all of us”). It’s pos­si­ble, but not inevitable.

If we mean the end of all life on earth, the fore­cast looks quite a bit rosier: we’ve prob­a­bly got about a bil­lion years, writes astro­physi­cist Jil­lian Scud­der, before the sun becomes “hot enough to boil our oceans.” Still not a cheer­ful thought, but per­haps many more crea­tures will take after the tardi­grade by then. That’s not even to men­tion nuclear war or the epi­demics, zom­bie and oth­er­wise, that could take us out.

But of course, for a not incon­sid­er­able num­ber of peo­ple, the ques­tion of the world’s end has noth­ing to do with sci­ence at all but with escha­tol­ogy, that branch of the­o­log­i­cal thought con­cerned with the Apoc­a­lypse.

The­o­log­i­cal thinkers have writ­ten about the Apoc­a­lypse for hun­dreds of years, and the world’s end was fre­quent­ly per­ceived as just around the cor­ner for many of the same rea­sons mod­ern sec­u­lar peo­ple feel apoc­a­lyp­tic dread: dis­ease, nat­ur­al dis­as­ters, wars, rumors of wars, impe­r­i­al pow­er strug­gles, uncom­fort­ably shift­ing demo­graph­ics….

Take 15th-cen­tu­ry Europe, when “the Apoc­a­lypse weighed heav­i­ly on the minds of the peo­ple,” as Bet­sy Mason and Greg Miller write at the Nation­al Geo­graph­ic blog All Over the Map: “Plagues were ram­pant. The once-great cap­i­tal of the Roman empire, Con­stan­tino­ple, had fall­en to the Turks. Sure­ly, the end was nigh.”

While a niche pub­lish­ing mar­ket in the nascent print era pro­duced “dozens of print­ed works” describ­ing the “com­ing reck­on­ing in gory detail… one long-for­got­ten man­u­script depicts the Apoc­a­lypse in a very dif­fer­ent way—through maps.” As you can see here, these maps con­vey the unfold­ing of worse-to-wors­er sce­nar­ios in a num­ber of visu­al reg­is­ters: tem­po­ral, sym­bol­ic, geo­graph­ic, the­mat­ic, etc.

At the top, the nest­ed tri­an­gles depict the rise of the Antichrist between the years 1570 and 1600. The cen­tral con­cern for this author was the sup­posed glob­al threat of Islam. Thus, the next map, its “T” shape a com­mon Medieval world map device, shows the world before the Apoc­a­lypse, the text around it explain­ing that “Islam is on the rise from 639 to 1514.”

Then, we have a cir­cu­lar map with five swords point­ing at the edges of the known world, illus­trat­ing the author’s con­tention that Islam­ic armies would reach the edges of the earth. The oth­er maps depict the “four horns of the Antichrist,” above, Judge­ment Day, below, (the black eye at the bot­tom is the “black abyss that leads to hell”), and, fur­ther down, a dia­gram describ­ing “the rel­a­tive diam­e­ters of Earth and Hell.”

Made in Lübeck, Ger­many some­time between 1486 and 1488, the man­u­script is writ­ten in Latin, “but it’s not as schol­ar­ly as oth­er con­tem­po­rary man­u­scripts,” write Mason and Miller, “and the pen­man­ship is fair­ly poor.” His­to­ri­an of car­tog­ra­phy Chet Van Duzer explains that “it’s aimed at the cul­tur­al elite, but not the pin­na­cle of the cul­tur­al elite.”

Point­ing out the obvi­ous, Van Duzer says, “there’s no way to escape it, this work is very anti-Islam­ic,” a wide­spread sen­ti­ment in medieval Europe, when the “clash of civ­i­liza­tions” nar­ra­tive spread its roots deep in cer­tain strains of West­ern think­ing. This par­tic­u­lar text also “includes a sec­tion on astro­log­i­cal med­i­cine and a trea­tise on geog­ra­phy that’s remark­ably ahead of its time.”

Van Duzer and Ilya Dines have stud­ied the rare man­u­script for its insight­ful pas­sages on geog­ra­phy and car­tog­ra­phy and pub­lished their research in a book titled Apoc­a­lyp­tic Car­tog­ra­phy. For all its the­o­log­i­cal alarmism, the man­u­script is sur­pris­ing­ly thought­ful when it comes to ana­lyz­ing its own for­mal prop­er­ties and per­spec­tives.

Mason and Miller note that “the author out­lines an essen­tial­ly mod­ern under­stand­ing of the­mat­ic maps as a means to illus­trate char­ac­ter­is­tics of the peo­ple or polit­i­cal orga­ni­za­tion of dif­fer­ent regions.” As Van Duzer puts it, “this is one of the most amaz­ing pas­sages, to have some­one from the 15th cen­tu­ry telling you their ideas about what maps can do.” This marks the work, he claims in the intro­duc­tion to Apoc­a­lyp­tic Car­tog­ra­phy, as that “of one of the most orig­i­nal car­tog­ra­phers of the peri­od.”

The Apoc­a­lypse Map now resides at the Hunt­ing­ton Library in Los Ange­les.

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2018.

entries.title: Discover the Lost Horror Series Deemed Too Shocking for BBC Television (1967)
entries.summary: High culture and new technology have never been a natural pairing. As our digital era has often underscored, media innovations tend to be adopted earliest to deliver the most puerile, sensation-driven content, with the more respectable stuff benefiting only later. When the BBC was introducing color broadcasting in the mid-nineteen-sixties, for instance, it was used […]
entries.content:
High cul­ture and new tech­nol­o­gy have nev­er been a nat­ur­al pair­ing. As our dig­i­tal era has often under­scored, media inno­va­tions tend to be adopt­ed ear­li­est to deliv­er the most puerile, sen­sa­tion-dri­ven con­tent, with the more respectable stuff ben­e­fit­ing only lat­er. When the BBC was intro­duc­ing col­or broad­cast­ing in the mid-nine­teen-six­ties, for instance, it was used for the likes of Thun­der­birds, The Avengers, and The Ben­ny Hill Show, respectable though those pro­grams may now seem com­pared to what main­stream tele­vi­sion would become in lat­er decades. No col­or pro­duc­tion of that peri­od aimed quite as low as the anthol­o­gy series Late Night Hor­ror — or has since been raised so high in the minds of those who remem­ber it.

“We must do every­thing we can from the very begin­ning to stim­u­late sus­pense, ten­sion, atmos­phere, poten­tial hor­ror and HORROR!” the show’s pro­duc­er Har­ry Moore wrote in a memo to his staff in 1967. “If there is blood, let’s see the blood.” Just a few years before choco­late syrup cir­cled the drain in Alfred Hitch­cock­’s Psy­cho, whose faint­ly anachro­nis­tic black-and-white cin­e­matog­ra­phy only inten­si­fied its scari­ness, Late Night Hor­ror had a man­date to paint the small screen red. As cul­tur­al leg­end has it, only six episodes were broad­cast before com­plaints about its pow­er to shock and dis­turb, or per­haps con­cerns about its increas­ing extrem­i­ty, got it the axe from BBC man­age­ment.

The idea that Late Night Hor­ror was sim­ply too scary for tele­vi­sion — or British pub­lic tele­vi­sion of the late six­ties, in any case — has become more com­pelling over the decades in part because so lit­tle of the series itself has sur­vived to receive the judg­ment of lat­er gen­er­a­tions of view­ers. Only in 2016 did archivists dis­cov­er a film copy of “The Corpse Can’t Play,” a sto­ry set at a chil­dren’s par­ty that takes a dead­ly turn. Writ­ten by the pro­lif­ic Eng­lish nov­el­ist John Burke, the episode’s slow burn leads up to a grotesque fin­ish that con­trasts almost cheek­i­ly with the mun­dane domes­tic­i­ty of its set­ting. Alas, the recov­ered print was in black-and-white, so we don’t get to see the col­ors, san­guineous and oth­er­wise, that would have made such an impact on view­ers of near­ly six decades ago.

Just this year, anoth­er episode was redis­cov­ered: “No Such Thing as a Vam­pire” by Richard Math­e­son, author of I Am Leg­end and no few­er than six­teen Twi­light Zone episodes. As of now, the oth­er four episodes remain miss­ing, and pre­sum­ably erased under the per­pet­u­al­ly cash-strapped BBC’s pol­i­cy of eras­ing tapes for re-use in the mid-twen­ti­eth cen­tu­ry. One of them, “William and Mary,” was based on a Roald Dahl sto­ry that had been pre­vi­ous­ly adapt­ed in 1961 for the series Way Out, and would be adapt­ed again in 1979 for Tales of the Unex­pect­ed. At this point, even if a com­plete set of Late Night Hor­ror tapes were to turn up in some­one’s shed, the real­i­ty of the show could hard­ly be expect­ed to com­pete with what its scat­tered frag­ments — espe­cial­ly its still-chill­ing open­ing sequence — inspire us to imag­ine. As every seri­ous hor­ror fan knows, it’s what we don’t see that scares us most.

via Men­tal Floss

entries.title: In 1704, Isaac Newton Predicted That the World Will End in 2060
entries.summary: We have become quite used to pronouncements of doom, from scientists predicting the sixth mass extinction due to the measurable effects of climate change, and from religionists declaring the apocalypse due to a surfeit of sin. It’s almost impossible to imagine these two groups of people agreeing on anything other than the ominous portent of […]
entries.content:
We have become quite used to pro­nounce­ments of doom, from sci­en­tists pre­dict­ing the sixth mass extinc­tion due to the mea­sur­able effects of cli­mate change, and from reli­gion­ists declar­ing the apoc­a­lypse due to a sur­feit of sin. It’s almost impos­si­ble to imag­ine these two groups of peo­ple agree­ing on any­thing oth­er than the omi­nous por­tent of their respec­tive mes­sages. But in the ear­ly days of the sci­en­tif­ic revolution—the days of Shake­speare’s con­tem­po­rary Fran­cis Bacon, and lat­er 17th cen­tu­ry Descartes—it was not at all unusu­al to find both kinds of rea­son­ing, or unrea­son­ing, in the same per­son, along with beliefs in mag­ic, div­ina­tion, astrol­o­gy, etc.

Yet even in this mael­strom of het­ero­dox thought and prac­tices, Sir Isaac New­ton stood out as a par­tic­u­lar­ly odd co-exis­tence of eso­teric bib­li­cal prophe­cy, occult beliefs, and a rigid, for­mal math­e­mat­ics that not only adhered to the induc­tive sci­en­tif­ic method, but also expand­ed its poten­tial by apply­ing gen­er­al axioms to spe­cif­ic cas­es.

Yet many of Newton’s gen­er­al prin­ci­ples would seem total­ly inim­i­cal to the nat­u­ral­ism of most physi­cists today. As he was for­mu­lat­ing the prin­ci­ples of grav­i­ty and three laws of motion, for exam­ple, New­ton also sought the leg­endary Philosopher’s Stone and attempt­ed to turn met­al to gold. More­over, the devout­ly reli­gious New­ton wrote the­o­log­i­cal trea­tis­es inter­pret­ing Bib­li­cal prophe­cies and pre­dict­ing the end of the world. The date he arrived at? 2060.

New­ton seems, writes sci­ence blog Anoth­er Pale Blue Dot, “as con­fi­dent of his pre­dic­tions in this realm as he was in the ratio­nal world of sci­ence.” In a 1704 let­ter exhib­it­ed at Jerusalem’s Hebrew Uni­ver­si­ty, above, New­ton describes his “rec­coning”:

So then the time times & half a time are 42 months or 1260 days or three years & an half, rec­coning twelve months to a yeare & 30 days to a month as was done in the Cal­en­dar of the prim­i­tive year. And the days of short lived Beasts being put for the years of lived [sic] king­doms, the peri­od of 1260 days, if dat­ed from the com­plete con­quest of the three kings A.C. 800, will end A.C. 2060. It may end lat­er, but I see no rea­son for its end­ing soon­er.

New­ton fur­ther demon­strates his con­fi­dence in the next sen­tence, writ­ing that his intent, “though not to assert” an answer, should in any event “put a stop the rash con­jec­tures of fan­ci­full men who are fre­quent­ly pre­dict­ing the time of the end.” Indeed. So how did he arrive at this num­ber? New­ton applied a rig­or­ous method, that is to be sure.

If you have the patience for an exhaus­tive descrip­tion of how he worked out his pre­dic­tion using the Book of Daniel, you may read one here by his­to­ri­an of sci­ence Stephen Sno­be­len, who also points out how wide­spread the inter­est in Newton’s odd beliefs has become, reach­ing across every con­ti­nent, though schol­ars have known about this side of the Enlight­en­ment giant for a long time.

For a sense of the exact­ing, yet com­plete­ly bizarre fla­vor of Newton’s prophet­ic cal­cu­la­tions, see anoth­er New­ton let­ter at the top of the post, tran­scribed below.

Prop. 1. The 2300 prophet­ick days did not com­mence before the rise of the lit­tle horn of the He Goat.

2 Those day [sic] did not com­mence a[f]ter the destruc­tion of Jerusalem & ye Tem­ple by the Romans A.[D.] 70.

3 The time times & half a time did not com­mence before the year 800 in wch the Popes suprema­cy com­menced

4 They did not com­mence after the re[ig]ne of Gre­go­ry the 7th. 1084

5 The 1290 days did not com­mence b[e]fore the year 842.

6 They did not com­mence after the reigne of Pope Greg. 7th. 1084

7 The dif­f­ence [sic] between the 1290 & 1335 days are a parts of the sev­en weeks.

There­fore the 2300 years do not end before ye year 2132 nor after 2370.

The time times & half time do n[o]t end before 2060 nor after [2344]

The 1290 days do not begin [this should read: end] before 2090 [New­ton might mean: 2132] nor after 1374 [sic; New­ton prob­a­bly means 2374]

The edi­to­r­i­al inser­tions are Pro­fes­sor Snobelen’s, who thinks the let­ter dates “from after 1705,” and that “the shaky hand­writ­ing sug­gests a date of com­po­si­tion late in Newton’s life.” What­ev­er the exact date, we see him much less cer­tain here; New­ton push­es around some oth­er dates—2344, 2090 (or 2132), 2374. All of them seem arbi­trary, but “giv­en the nice round­ness of the num­ber,” writes Moth­er­board, “and the fact that it appears in more than one let­ter,” 2060 has become his most mem­o­rable dat­ing for the apoc­a­lypse.

It’s impor­tant to note that New­ton didn’t believe the world would “end” in the sense of cease to exist or burn up in holy flames. His end times phi­los­o­phy resem­bles that of a sur­pris­ing num­ber of cur­rent day evan­gel­i­cals: Christ would return and reign for a mil­len­ni­um, the Jew­ish dias­po­ra would return to Israel and would, he wrote, set up “a flour­ish­ing and ever­last­ing King­dom.” We hear such state­ments often from tel­e­van­ge­lists, school boards, gov­er­nors, and pres­i­den­tial can­di­dates.

As many peo­ple have argued, despite Newton’s con­cep­tion of his sci­en­tif­ic work as a bul­wark against oth­er the­olo­gies, it ulti­mate­ly became a foun­da­tion for Deism and Nat­u­ral­ism, and has allowed sci­en­tists to make accu­rate pre­dic­tions for hun­dreds of years. 20th cen­tu­ry physics may have shown us a much more rad­i­cal­ly unsta­ble uni­verse than New­ton ever imag­ined, but his the­o­ries are, as Isaac Asi­mov would put it, “not so much wrong as incom­plete,” and still essen­tial to our under­stand­ing of cer­tain fun­da­men­tal phe­nom­e­na. But as fas­ci­nat­ing and curi­ous as Newton’s oth­er inter­ests may be, there’s no more rea­son to cred­it his prophet­ic cal­cu­la­tions than those of the Mil­lerites, Harold Camp­ing, or any oth­er apoc­a­lyp­tic dooms­day sect.

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2015.

entries.title: 300 Years Before ChatGPT, Jonathan Swift’s Gulliver’s Travels Imagined Machines Writing Books and Producing Knowledge (1726)
entries.summary: The printing press was invented in the middle of the fifteenth century, and it’s been downhill for the written word ever since. Even before then, arguments that the volume of writing being done far outstripped the value of that writing surely weren’t unheard of. Whatever the era, the most incisive remarks on the apparent victory […]
entries.content:
The print­ing press was invent­ed in the mid­dle of the fif­teenth cen­tu­ry, and it’s been down­hill for the writ­ten word ever since. Even before then, argu­ments that the vol­ume of writ­ing being done far out­stripped the val­ue of that writ­ing sure­ly weren’t unheard of. What­ev­er the era, the most inci­sive remarks on the appar­ent vic­to­ry of ver­bal quan­ti­ty over ver­bal qual­i­ty tend to have come from writ­ers them­selves. No less a satirist than Jonathan Swift made it one of his many tar­gets in Gul­liv­er’s Trav­els (1726), imag­in­ing an elab­o­rate machine of wood and wire called “the Engine” (see illus­tra­tion above) that auto­mat­i­cal­ly gen­er­ates text, though few remem­ber it — or rather, few remem­bered it until the rise of large lan­guage mod­els in the real world.

Gul­liv­er encoun­ters that tech­no­log­i­cal mar­vel, the Engine, at an insti­tu­tion called the Acad­e­my of Pro­jec­tors in the city of Laga­do. Swift’s pro­tag­o­nist records its cre­ator’s expla­na­tion as fol­lows: “Every one knew how labo­ri­ous the usu­al method is of attain­ing to arts and sci­ences; where­as, by his con­trivance, the most igno­rant per­son, at a rea­son­able charge, and with a lit­tle bod­i­ly labor, might write books in phi­los­o­phy, poet­ry, pol­i­tics, laws, math­e­mat­ics, and the­ol­o­gy, with­out the least assis­tance from genius or study.” The Engine’s oper­a­tion, with its unwieldy, clack­ing com­po­nents and a scram­bling staff of young crankers, read­ers, and scribes, may strike us as bizarre, just as it did audi­ences in the eigh­teenth cen­tu­ry. But in our time, when stu­dents can write their papers lit­er­al­ly with­out giv­ing it a thought (to say noth­ing of what their pro­fes­sors may be get­ting up to), its con­cept now sounds all too plau­si­ble.

“This is one of the ear­li­est known men­tions of a machine that could be con­sid­ered as a com­put­er in lit­er­a­ture, more than a hun­dred years pri­or to the first cal­cu­lat­ing engine designs by Charles Bab­bage,” writes Chris Gar­cia at the web site of the Com­put­er His­to­ry Muse­um. “The Engine might be seen as a com­put­er, but per­haps it’s bet­ter thought of as a sort of ran­dom-num­ber gen­er­a­tor,” spout­ing out whichev­er words of the local lan­guage that cor­re­spond with the dig­its. That post dates from ten years, near­ly to the day, before the launch of Chat­G­PT, which changed the gen­er­al pub­lic’s ideas about what com­put­ers can and can’t do. We may dis­agree about whether a machine can tru­ly gen­er­ate “a com­plete body of all arts and sci­ences,” as the Engine’s inven­tor intends, but it no longer sounds like sheer­est fan­ta­sy.

Swift had in mind not engi­neers of arti­fi­cial intel­li­gence but the Roy­al Soci­ety, whose enthu­si­asm for sci­en­tif­ic knowl­edge and exper­i­men­ta­tion he saw as insuf­fi­cient­ly teth­ered to real­i­ty, or at least prac­ti­cal­i­ty. In addi­tion to the Engine, writes lit­er­a­ture pro­fes­sor Robin Bates, “Swift imag­ines sci­en­tists attempt­ing to extract sun­beams from cucum­bers, soft­en mar­ble into pil­lows and pin­cush­ions, replace silk­worms with spi­ders (and hav­ing them eat bright­ly col­ored flies so the threads will be pre-dyed), mix paint by smell, reassem­ble orig­i­nal food stuffs from excre­ment, and build hous­es from the top down (in imi­ta­tion of the bee and the spi­der).” His satire holds up today thanks to his under­stand­ing that, “for all the promis­es of the Enlight­en­ment, the Age of Rea­son, and the Sci­en­tif­ic and Tech­no­log­i­cal Rev­o­lu­tions,” our attempts to change the world “founder the moment we start ignor­ing human nature.” But who needs human nature, the Pro­jec­tors of today might argue, when you’ve got enough com­pute?

entries.title: Artists Frida Kahlo & Diego Rivera Visit Leon Trotsky in Mexico: Vintage Footage from 1938
entries.summary: Here’s some rare footage of the great Mexican painters Diego Rivera and Frida Kahlo paying a visit to exiled Soviet revolutionary Leon Trotsky and his wife, Natalia Sedova, in Coyoacán, Mexico, in 1938. The Trotskys had arrived the year before, after Rivera petitioned the government of President Lázaro Cárdenas to grant the controversial Marxist leader and theorist sanctuary in Mexico. When […]
entries.content:
Here’s some rare footage of the great Mex­i­can painters Diego Rivera and Fri­da Kahlo pay­ing a vis­it to exiled Sovi­et rev­o­lu­tion­ary Leon Trot­sky and his wife, Natalia Sedo­va, in Coyoacán, Mex­i­co, in 1938.

The Trot­skys had arrived the year before, after Rivera peti­tioned the gov­ern­ment of Pres­i­dent Lázaro Cár­de­nas to grant the con­tro­ver­sial Marx­ist leader and the­o­rist sanc­tu­ary in Mex­i­co. When the Trot­skys arrived on a Nor­we­gian oil tanker at the port city of Tampi­co in Jan­u­ary of 1937, Rivera was not well, but Kahlo board­ed the ship to wel­come the Trot­skys and accom­pa­nied them on an armored train to Mex­i­co City. She invit­ed the Trot­skys to stay at her fam­i­ly home, La Casa Azul (the Blue House) in Coyoacán, now a sec­tion of Mex­i­co City. By the time this footage was tak­en by a vis­it­ing Amer­i­can named Ivan Heisler, Trot­sky and Kahlo had either had, or were about to have, a brief affair, and the friend­ship between the two cou­ples would soon fall apart. In ear­ly 1939 Trot­sky moved to anoth­er house in the same neigh­bor­hood, where he was assas­si­nat­ed in August of 1940.

entries.title: When Buckminster Fuller Proposed Putting a Dome Over Manhattan (1960)
entries.summary: Image via Buckminster Fuller Estate The novels of John Brunner have become a niche taste, even within his genre of science fiction. A more sociologically minded version of Philip K. Dick at his best, he could write with what now looks like a simultaneous prescience about the civilization to come and an apocalyptically anxious concern […]
entries.content:
Image via Buck­min­ster Fuller Estate

The nov­els of John Brun­ner have become a niche taste, even with­in his genre of sci­ence fic­tion. A more soci­o­log­i­cal­ly mind­ed ver­sion of Philip K. Dick at his best, he could write with what now looks like a simul­ta­ne­ous pre­science about the civ­i­liza­tion to come and an apoc­a­lyp­ti­cal­ly anx­ious con­cern with the issues of his day. His undis­put­ed mas­ter­piece Stand on Zanz­ibar came out in 1968, the same year as the late Paul R. Ehrlich’s The Pop­u­la­tion Bomb. Both books deal with the dire con­se­quences of what, at the time, looked like the run­away mul­ti­pli­ca­tion of human­i­ty, though ele­ments of the dystopi­an sci-fi writer’s vision now look rather more cred­i­ble than the pre­dic­tions of the Stan­ford biol­o­gist — apart from the giant geo­des­ic dome cov­er­ing Man­hat­tan, any­way.

In a sense, Brun­ner was actu­al­ly behind the times, since Buck­min­ster Fuller him­self had sug­gest­ed dom­ing Man­hat­tan near­ly a decade ear­li­er. In their ambi­tious pro­pos­al for a “two-mile-wide Dome Over Man­hat­tan” from the turn of the nine­teen-six­ties, Fuller and long­time col­lab­o­ra­tor Sho­ji Sadao “imag­ined a mas­sive archi­tec­tur­al sur­face that would reg­u­late the city’s ecosys­tems,” write Next City’s Janette Kim and Erik Carv­er. “They deliv­ered this design along with a series of sur­pris­ing cal­cu­la­tions: the Dome would reduce heat loss by scal­ing the city to one eighty-fifth of its sur­face area; the elim­i­na­tion of snow­plow­ing alone would pay for heat; build­ings inside the Dome could be built lighter and cheap­er with­out need for weath­er­proof­ing; and inte­ri­or air could be heat­ed by remote plants.”

Fuller and Sadao did bring some num­bers to back up their claims, but even more impor­tant­ly, they made assur­ances that the dome’s glass would be one-way, a defense against pry­ing non-Man­hat­tan­ite eyes, and would keep res­i­dents’ cars and lawns in prime con­di­tion. How­ev­er out­landish­ly for­ward-think­ing Fuller could be, he nev­er for­got that he need­ed to appeal to the wor­ries and aspi­ra­tions of mid-cen­tu­ry Amer­i­ca. As a per­son­al­i­ty, he also fit in well with the era’s enthu­si­asm for sweep­ing infra­struc­tur­al fix­es. “It was a time when peo­ple real­ly believed in the pow­er of tech­nol­o­gy,” says Nev­er Built New York co-author Sam Lubell. “We’re build­ing space­ships that go to the moon. Why can’t we build a dome over Man­hat­tan to get rid of all this pol­lu­tion, get rid of all the prob­lems of weath­er?”

Still, as eccen­tric as he was, Fuller was­n’t delu­sion­al. “It’d be very worth­while to have cities under geo­des­ic domes, but New York City, if you think about all the dif­fer­ent own­ers of dif­fer­ent lands, the con­tro­ver­sy about ‘this is my air rights, I don’t want a thing over my thing here,’ I just don’t think it’s going to hap­pen,” he admit­ted. But “it can hap­pen where you start out in places where ener­gy is a real­ly fan­tas­tic prob­lem.” At the time, the ever-increas­ing demand for resources of all kinds by a rapid­ly grow­ing pop­u­la­tion appeared to be not just a but the fan­tas­tic prob­lem. Today, once-unfore­see­able devel­op­ments like ris­ing ener­gy effi­cien­cy and an appar­ent­ly inex­orable decline in glob­al birthrates have direct­ed our ner­vous gazes else­where. Yet dat­ed visions of tech­no­log­i­cal utopia and dystopia still strike us as odd­ly famil­iar — and indeed, as strange­ly sim­i­lar to one anoth­er.

Relat­ed con­tent:

entries.title: LEGO Lets You Build Gaudí’s Sagrada Família in Its Largest Set Ever
entries.summary: When work on the Sagrada Família first began in 1882, the original architect could hardly have imagined that, 144 years later, the ambitious undertaking would still be underway. Yet here we are. Famously, the Catalan architect Antoni Gaudí (1852–1926) spent the last four decades of his life designing and building the Gothic-inspired basilica in Barcelona. […]
entries.content:
When work on the Sagra­da Família first began in 1882, the orig­i­nal archi­tect could hard­ly have imag­ined that, 144 years lat­er, the ambi­tious under­tak­ing would still be under­way. Yet here we are. Famous­ly, the Cata­lan archi­tect Antoni Gaudí (1852–1926) spent the last four decades of his life design­ing and build­ing the Goth­ic-inspired basil­i­ca in Barcelona. Then came the Span­ish Civ­il War (1936–1939), which destroyed many of his archi­tec­tur­al plans, leav­ing suc­ces­sive gen­er­a­tions of archi­tects to piece togeth­er Gaudí’s vision and move the project for­ward. At long last, ear­li­er this year, builders com­plet­ed the cen­tral Tow­er of Jesus Christ, which stands 566 feet high, mak­ing the Sagra­da Família the tallest church in the world.

Although work on the Glo­ry façade still remains, the basil­i­ca has reached a near-com­plete state—complete enough for Lego to roll out the offi­cial Sagra­da Família Lego set. At 12,060 pieces, it’s the largest Lego set ever made, and it lets you build the Sagra­da Família sec­tion by sec­tion, fol­low­ing the same order as the orig­i­nal archi­tects. “Your build­ing jour­ney begins with the Apse with Crypt, the Nativ­i­ty façade and the Pas­sion façade. It then moves on to the naves and the West­ern Sac­risty. Com­plete the 6 tow­ers and fin­ish the basil­i­ca with the East­ern Sac­risty and the Glo­ry façade.” With the video above, you can watch the build­ing of the Lego basil­i­ca, com­press­ing hours of work into 10 min­utes. The Lego set will be avail­able on Novem­ber 1, 2026.
